candidates.quote: May lily-dotted lakes delight your eye; / May shade-trees bid the heat of noonday cease; / May soft winds blow the lotus-pollen nigh; / May all your path be pleasantness and peace.
candidates.author: Kālidāsa
candidates.locator: Act IV, spoken by invisible beings as Shakuntala sets out from the hermitage, just after Kanva’s address to the trees and Sharngarava’s answer; Kalidasa: Translations of Shakuntala and Other Works, trans. Arthur W. Ryder (Everyman’s Library no. 629, J. M. Dent, London, and E. P. Dutton, New York, first issue of this edition 1912), Act IV; text checked word for word in Project Gutenberg ebook 16659, a transcription of that Everyman volume; the fourth act is the act the Sanskrit tradition singles out, though the four stanzas its tag verse names do not include this blessing
candidates.whyThisMonth: A blessing for someone leaving home on a long road: cool lakes, shade at noon, a kind wind, and a path that is pleasant the whole way.
candidates.speaker: Invisible beings
candidates.year: c. 400 (composed; the date is inferred from tradition, not documented)

candidates.quote: When I woke up to-day and got up and dressed myself, I suddenly began to feel as if everything in this life was open to me, and that I knew how I must live.
candidates.author: Anton Chekhov
candidates.locator: Act I, Irina to Ivan Romanovitch (Chebutikin) on her name-day, the sentence that opens the speech ending ‘A man must work, toil in the sweat of his brow’; Plays by Anton Chekhov, Second Series, trans. Julius West (Charles Scribner’s Sons, 1916); text: Project Gutenberg ebook 7986, whose title page names West; the speech is a standing audition piece, but no entry in a printed reference was opened this run
candidates.whyThisMonth: A young woman wakes on a spring morning and finds, for one hour, that the whole of her life looks open and she knows how to live it.
candidates.speaker: Irina
candidates.year: 1901 (first performed at the Moscow Art Theatre and first printed)

candidates.quote: And this our life, exempt from public haunt, / Finds tongues in trees, books in the running brooks, / Sermons in stones, and good in everything.
candidates.author: William Shakespeare
candidates.locator: Act 2, scene 1, lines 15 to 17, Folger Shakespeare Library edition, the Duke’s first speech in the Forest of Arden, following ‘Sweet are the uses of adversity’; text read from the Folger Digital Texts file, which prints ‘everything’ as one word and closes the sentence with a full stop; a standing entry in Bartlett’s Familiar Quotations; Shakespeare stands at two of three in the year
candidates.whyThisMonth: A banished duke finds that the woods he was driven into have turned into his teachers, which is the month’s claim about any road you did not choose.
candidates.speaker: Duke Senior

candidates.quote: Released from ice are brook and river / By the quickening glance of the gracious Spring; / The colors of hope to the valley cling, / And weak old Winter himself must shiver, / Withdrawn to the mountains, a crownless king.
candidates.author: Johann Wolfgang von Goethe
candidates.work: Faust: A Tragedy, The First Part
candidates.locator: Before the City Gate, the opening of Faust’s Easter walk speech to Wagner (German: Vom Eise befreit sind Strom und Bäche, lines 903 to 907 by the standard numbering, which was not checked against a numbered edition this run); trans. Bayard Taylor, first published 1870; text: Project Gutenberg ebook 14591, an illustrated reprint of Taylor’s Part One; Taylor ends line 5 with a colon and the sentence runs on, so the closing full stop is the cut, at a complete clause; the Osterspaziergang is a standing entry in Büchmann’s Geflügelte Worte
candidates.whyThisMonth: The most quoted thaw in German: the ice lets go of the water, hope gets its colour back in the valley, and winter retreats uphill with no crown left.
candidates.speaker: Faust

candidates.quote: You see things; and you say ‘Why?’ But I dream things that never were; and I say ‘Why not?’ I made the word dead to describe my old skin that I cast when I am renewed. I call that renewal being born.
candidates.author: Bernard Shaw
candidates.work: Back to Methuselah: A Metabiological Pentateuch
candidates.locator: Part I, In the Beginning, Act I, the Serpent to Eve in the Garden; Back to Methuselah (Constable, 1921); text: Project Gutenberg ebook 13084, which prints single quotation marks around Why and Why not; the first sentence is the line Bartlett’s carries and the one Robert Kennedy made famous in 1968, and the two sentences after it are the Serpent’s own gloss on renewal
candidates.whyThisMonth: The Serpent answers Eve’s question about what birth is by pointing at her own cast skin: the dreaming of what never was and the shedding of the old are the same act, called being born.
candidates.speaker: The Serpent

candidates.quote: Wanderer, your footsteps are / the road, and nothing more; / wanderer, there is no road, / the road is made by walking.
candidates.author: Antonio Machado
candidates.work: Proverbios y cantares XXIX (Proverbs and Songs XXIX), Campos de Castilla
candidates.locator: lines 1 to 4; Selected Poems of Antonio Machado, trans. Betty Jean Craige (Louisiana State University Press, 1978), p. 143; CONFIDENCE MEDIUM: the page was not opened, and this wording with that page credit is taken from two later books that cite Craige 1978, p. 143, so the line breaks here follow the Spanish quatrain and must be checked against the printed page before landing; which printing first carried XXIX, the 1912 Campos de Castilla or the 1917 Poesías completas, was also not settled this run
candidates.whyThisMonth: The line every Spanish speaker knows, and the plainest statement of this month: there is no road waiting for you, there is only the walking that makes one.

candidates.quote: I awake light-hearted this morning of spring, / Everywhere round me the singing of birds— / But now I remember the night, the storm, / And I wonder how many blossoms were broken.
candidates.author: Meng Haoran
candidates.locator: the complete quatrain; The Jade Mountain: A Chinese Anthology, Being Three Hundred Poems of the T’ang Dynasty, trans. Witter Bynner from the texts of Kiang Kang-hu (Alfred A. Knopf, 1929), p. 152; text read from the scan-backed Wikisource transcription of that page, which sets the dash after ‘birds’; one of the best known poems in Chinese, and the opening piece of the Qianjiashi school anthology
candidates.whyThisMonth: The oldest six in the morning poem there is: you wake glad in spring with birds all round, and only then remember the storm that went through in the night.

candidates.quote: I will mount a long wind some day and break the heavy waves / And set my cloudy sail straight and bridge the deep, deep sea.
candidates.author: Li Bai
candidates.locator: the closing two lines, after the refrain ‘Journeying is hard, / Journeying is hard. / There are many turnings’; The Jade Mountain: A Chinese Anthology, Being Three Hundred Poems of the T’ang Dynasty, trans. Witter Bynner from the texts of Kiang Kang-hu (Alfred A. Knopf, 1929); text read from the scan-backed Wikisource transcription; the Chinese couplet is a standing proverb of perseverance
candidates.whyThisMonth: After a poem that says four times over how hard the road is, the last two lines put the sail up anyway and head for open water.

candidates.quote: The time that my journey takes is long and the way of it long. I came out on the chariot of the first gleam of light, and pursued my voyage through the wildernesses of worlds leaving my track on many a star and planet.
candidates.author: Rabindranath Tagore
candidates.locator: poem 12, the opening two paragraphs, in the author’s own English (The India Society, London, 1912; Macmillan, 1913); text: Project Gutenberg ebook 7164; Gitanjali is the book the 1913 Nobel Prize named, and this is prose-poetry, so it is given unbroken; the precedent for the form is the landed Gitanjali poem 10 line
candidates.whyThisMonth: Whoever set out at first light is still going, and the poem treats the length of the way as the point rather than the complaint.

candidates.quote: Oh, to be in England / Now that April’s there, / And who wakes in England / Sees, some morning, unaware, / That the lowest boughs and the brush-wood sheaf / Round the elm-tree bole are in tiny leaf, / While the chaffinch sings on the orchard bough / In England—now!
candidates.author: Robert Browning
candidates.locator: stanza I, lines 1 to 8, the whole first section; Bells and Pomegranates No. VII: Dramatic Romances and Lyrics (Edward Moxon, 1845); text read from the scan-backed Wikisource transcription of that printing, which reads ‘And who wakes in England’ where the later collected texts read ‘And whoever wakes in England’
candidates.whyThisMonth: An exile in Italy wants one thing only: to be the person who wakes in April and notices, before he is properly awake, that the lowest branches have gone into leaf.

candidates.quote: Does the road wind up-hill all the way? / Yes, to the very end. / Will the day’s journey take the whole long day? / From morn to night, my friend.
candidates.author: Christina Rossetti
candidates.locator: lines 1 to 4, the first stanza; first printed in Macmillan’s Magazine, February 1861, and collected in Goblin Market and Other Poems (Macmillan, 1862); text: Goblin Market, The Prince’s Progress, and Other Poems (Macmillan), Project Gutenberg ebook 16950; the poem is read as an allegory of the whole of a life, with the inn at the end as death, and the stanza quoted here is the road itself
candidates.whyThisMonth: Two questions anyone can ask at six in the morning, answered without flinching and without gloom: yes, uphill, and yes, all day.

candidates.quote: A little madness in the Spring / Is wholesome even for the King, / But God be with the Clown, / Who ponders this tremendous scene— / This whole experiment of green, / As if it were his own!
candidates.author: Emily Dickinson
candidates.work: ‘A little madness in the Spring’ (Franklin 1356, Johnson 1333)
candidates.locator: the complete poem; The Single Hound: Poems of a Lifetime, ed. Martha Dickinson Bianchi (Little, Brown, 1914), Part II; text read from the scan-backed Wikisource transcription of that edition, which prints ‘madness’ and ‘experiment of green’ in lower case and a comma after ‘Clown’, where modern editions from the manuscripts print capitals and a dash; Dickinson stands at two of three in the year
candidates.whyThisMonth: Dickinson hands the whole green experiment to the clown who takes it personally, which is the only sane way to meet an April morning.

candidates.quote: The world stands out on either side / No wider than the heart is wide; / Above the world is stretched the sky,— / No higher than the soul is high.
candidates.author: Edna St. Vincent Millay
candidates.locator: lines 203 to 206, counted in the printed text, in the closing passage after the speaker is given her life back; Renascence and Other Poems (Mitchell Kennerley, 1917); text read from the scan-backed Wikisource transcription of that edition, whose line 205 carries the comma and dash as set here; first printed in The Lyric Year (Mitchell Kennerley, 1912); the fame claim rests on the currency of these four lines and the standing of the poem, not on a reference entry opened this run
candidates.whyThisMonth: The measuring that follows a rebirth: the world is exactly as wide as the heart you meet it with, and the sky exactly as high as the soul.

candidates.quote: The roofs are shining from the rain, / The sparrows twitter as they fly, / And with a windy April grace / The little clouds go by. / Yet the back-yards are bare and brown / With only one unchanging tree— / I could not be so sure of Spring / Save that it sings in me.
candidates.author: Sara Teasdale
candidates.locator: the complete poem, eight lines; Rivers to the Sea (Macmillan, 1915); text: Project Gutenberg ebook 596, a transcription of that edition, which sets the dash after ‘tree’ and opens with a display capital on ‘The’
candidates.whyThisMonth: Wet roofs, bare yards, nothing much to look at: the proof of spring this morning is that it is singing inside the person looking.

candidates.quote: And the miraculous comes so close / to the ruined, dirty houses— / something not known to anyone at all, / but wild in our breast for centuries.
candidates.author: Anna Akhmatova
candidates.work: ‘Everything is plundered’ (Vsyo raskhishcheno, predano, prodano, 1921), from Anno Domini MCMXXI
candidates.locator: the closing stanza, lines 9 to 12; Poems of Akhmatova, selected and translated by Stanley Kunitz with Max Hayward (Little, Brown, 1973); wording and lineation checked against several credited reprints of that translation rather than the printed page, so confidence is medium; the poem opens on the loss and asks why we do not despair, and the two stanzas after that, of which this is the second, are the answer
candidates.whyThisMonth: Written in a wrecked city in 1921, and still the plainest account of renewal: the miraculous comes right up to the damaged houses, wanting in.

candidates.quote: I got out of bed / on two strong legs. / It might have been / otherwise. I ate / cereal, sweet / milk, ripe, flawless / peach. It might / have been otherwise.
candidates.author: Jane Kenyon
candidates.locator: lines 1 to 8, the opening; Otherwise: New and Selected Poems (Graywolf Press, 1996), the new poems, which Kenyon selected and arranged shortly before her death in April 1995; lineation checked against two reprints of the Graywolf text, not the printed page, so confidence is medium; the quotation stops at the end of line 8, and the poem goes on to the day’s work and closes on the knowledge that one day it will be otherwise
candidates.whyThisMonth: Getting up and eating breakfast, counted out as the gifts they are, which is as much renewal as most mornings are asked to carry.
